documents.title: Standard for Acceptable Use of Artificial Intelligence with University Data
documents.summary: IT standard for all JMU users on acceptable and ethical AI use with university data. It names Copilot Chat as the one approved GenAI tool, requires IT review for others, and sets data-protection, validation and disclosure duties. It leaves classroom rules to separate 'AI in Education' guidance.
documents.stance_why: The standard says JMU 'supports responsible use and experimentation with AI tools' and lets users use Copilot Chat freely, with conditions on data, tool approval and disclosure; it bans only DeepSeek and Highly Confidential Data. It does not delegate or ban, so permit.

units.why: Defines the standard's scope: it binds 'all JMU users (faculty, staff, & students)' and covers embedded and generative AI, so it is an institution-level framework (P56) rather than a definition-only unit (P61).
units.anchor: requirements for all JMU users (faculty, staff, & students) on the acceptable and ethical use

units.why: Scope sentence lists stand-alone, embedded and generative AI, third-party AI and procurement; it sets what the policy covers, so P61.

units.why: Defines 'Artificial Intelligence (AI)' as machine simulation of human intelligence using machine learning; a definition that fixes what the policy covers, so P61.

units.policy: AI is defined as the simulation of human intelligence processes by machines, especially computer systems, such that it can adapt and learn on its own using machine learning algorithms

units.why: Defines 'Generative AI' as AI that can 'generate new content, such as text images, and audio'; a scope definition, P61.
units.anchor: A type of artificial intelligence that can learn from and mimic large amounts of data

units.why: Names Microsoft Copilot Chat as 'the only GenAI tool currently approved' for the whole community, i.e. a sanctioned licensed tool (P17); it is also the vetted-tool preference but P17 fits as the university provides it.

documents.title: Academic Integrity, Syllabi Statements and AI (Artificial Intelligence in Education guide)
documents.summary: Library research guide advising instructors to write syllabus statements, pick one of five AI-use levels per assignment, and favor process evidence over AI detectors. It is advice rather than binding policy.
documents.stance_why: The guide sets no rule itself: it tells instructors to 'Choose a level for each assignment' using a five-level scale and to post their own policy, so the decision rests with instructors, hence delegates with tiers.

units.why: Frames the guide's purpose: expectations should 'truly support student learning and cognitive gain'; no narrower type fits, so it is coded as framework preamble, P56.
units.anchor: Clear expectations in classes are supposed to truly support student learning and cognitive gain.

units.why: Cites the Critical AI Literacy principle that AI 'shouldn't replace' writing and thinking and students 'should still do substantial writing and reflection of their own'; student remains thinker, P32.
units.anchor: shouldn’t replace either, and students who use it should still do substantial writing and reflection
